I can help!! privmsg me if you like. In most cameras, you can ask the camera to "do the correct exposure" while you control one of the variables: sensitivity, exposure time, and aperture diameter. In the case of these pictures, the easiest way to start is to choose to control the time value, and then to make the exposure long. In my experience, getting the "fine mist" sort of look takes at least one second of exposure.

If you're prepared for something more advanced, then you may notice that the picture appears to be in focus from front to back. If you control both the aperture value and the film sensitivity, then you can make the aperture small (less light means longer exposure needed) and you can ALSO make the film very un-sensitive. These things combined allow you to leave the shutter open for a very long time.

As a result, you can get this sort of picture, that represents the "average" light dissipation of all the places water droplets might go.
